title: Why a Bee Stinger Pumps Venom for 70 Seconds Alone 🐝
description:
What actually happens when a bee stings you? A honeybee's barbed stinger saws itself into your skin, tears away with its venom sac, muscles and nerves, and keeps pumping venom on its own, while melittin sets off your pain nerves and an alarm scent that smells like bananas calls in more bees.

topic: What actually happens when a bee stings you?
script:
Why does a bee stinger keep pumping venom into you for up to seventy seconds,
after the bee flies away?
It's ripped out of her body, and it still works on its own.
So what actually happens in those few seconds after a sting?
Let's take it apart, one tiny piece at a time.
Part one. A saw that started as an egg tube.
Only female bees can sting.
That's because the stinger began as an egg-laying tube,
and male bees, called drones, don't have one at all.
Look closely and it isn't a needle.
It's three parts sliding together.
A central shaft called the stylet,
and two thin blades called lancets.
Each lancet is covered in backward-pointing barbs,
like the teeth on a tiny saw.
Part two. The stinger that walks itself in.
The two lancets slide up and down, one after the other.
One grips with its barbs, the other pushes deeper,
so the stinger actually walks itself into your skin.
And here's the wild part.
When the bee pulls away, the barbs hold tight,
and she leaves behind the whole pumping kit.
The venom sac, the muscles, and a little bundle of nerves.
In 2026, scientists filmed stingers in clear skin-like gel.
They saw a double piston pump.
Two pistons pushing in turns,
so venom only ever flows one way, into you.
The strong pumping kept going for fifteen to seventy seconds,
with no bee attached.
Part three. Why it hurts so much.
Up to half of dry bee venom is one ingredient, called melittin.
Melittin punches tiny holes in the cells it touches.
It also flips on your pain nerves and keeps them firing,
like someone leaning on a doorbell.
Then your body fights back.
It floods the spot with fluid from your blood to wash the venom away,
and that's the red, puffy bump you get.
Part four. Why the bee doesn't make it.
Your skin is thick and stretchy,
so those barbs can't slide back out.
When the bee flies off,
part of her belly tears away with the stinger.
She dies soon after.
But honeybees didn't evolve to sting us.
They usually fight other insects,
and a thin insect shell lets the stinger pull right out.
Wasps and bumblebees have smoother stingers,
so they can sting again and again.
Part five. A sting that calls for backup.
A sting also releases an alarm scent,
and it smells a lot like bananas.
To other bees, that smell means one thing.
Danger, right here.
It tags you as the target, so more bees can find you.
That's why bees act like a team.
One worker gives up her life,
and the whole hive stays protected.
And here's what scientists found about that leftover stinger.
Scraping it off or pinching it out works about the same.
What matters is speed.
Every second it stays in, it pumps a little more.
Next time, find out why your stomach is full of acid strong enough to eat through some metals,
and still doesn't digest itself.
key_facts: Only female bees (workers and queens) sting; the stinger is a modified egg-laying tube (ovipositor); drones have none
The stinger is a central stylet plus two barbed lancets that slide alternately and drive it deeper
A detached honeybee stinger keeps pumping: UNSW (Oct 2026) filmed strong regular pumping for 15-70 seconds, via a double-piston pump
Melittin is about 40-60% of dry honeybee venom; it forms pores in cells and activates pain receptors
Redness and swelling come from fluid released from the blood to flush the venom
Barbs catch in thick mammal skin, so the honeybee's abdomen ruptures and she dies; she can usually sting insects and pull free
Wasps and bumblebees have smooth stingers and can sting repeatedly
The alarm pheromone (isoamyl acetate) smells like bananas and recruits other bees
Scraping vs pinching makes no real difference; removing the stinger quickly is what matters
